samples.result:
# The Undirected Path: In Praise of Wandering

It begins with a small act of resistance: leaving your phone at home, taking a street you have never taken, letting an afternoon dissolve without a plan. In a culture that worships productivity, efficiency, and the relentless optimization of every waking hour, such acts can feel almost guilty. We have been taught that time is money, that goals must be set and milestones hit, that the shortest route between two points is always the best route. But the shortest route is not the richest route. The most memorable journeys, both inward and outward, are rarely the ones we could have mapped in advance. Wandering—geographical, intellectual, emotional—is not a failure of purpose. It is a different kind of purpose, one that refuses to mistake motion for meaning.

I remember being a child and wandering the woods behind my grandparents’ house. There was no destination. The point was simply to see what lay beyond the next bend, to follow a creek until it disappeared into a thicket, to notice the way light fell through the leaves. I never carried a watch. I never had a plan. And yet those hours were not empty. They were full of an alertness that structured time differently, not as a line with points to check off but as a texture to be explored. Something similar happens when we daydream, when we look out a train window and let our thoughts drift. We are often told this is wasted time. But the mind is not a machine that idles in neutral. It is a landscape, and wandering is how we discover its hidden valleys.

The modern attention economy is designed to prevent that discovery. Every screen, every notification, every algorithm is engineered to keep us engaged, to predict what we will want and give it to us before we even ask. We scroll through feeds that are curated by invisible mathematics, each post a tiny hook, each video a momentary surge of dopamine. We are told we are free—free to choose, free to browse, free to express ourselves—but the space of our attention is increasingly fenced. We are not wandering through a forest of possibility. We are walking down a corridor that has already been built for us, with walls that close in if we linger too long. The paradox of the algorithms is that they offer us more than we could ever consume, yet they narrow our sense of what is possible. They show us more of the same. They flatten surprise.

Boredom, once a natural state of the open mind, has become a problem to be solved. If you are on a long bus ride, you take out your phone. If you are standing in line, you scroll. If you are waiting for a friend, you refresh. The empty spaces of the day are filled before they can speak. But boredom is not the enemy of imagination; it is its antechamber. When the mind has nothing immediate to do, it begins to wander by itself. It rearranges the day’s fragments, tests odd combinations, returns to unfinished thoughts, dreams up questions that no one asked. Many of our best ideas arrive precisely when we are not trying to have them—in the shower, on a walk, in the half-light before sleep. The great mathematicians and poets have known this for centuries. Archimedes found his principle in a bath, not at a desk. Newton spoke of thinking by keeping a problem before him “for a long time, patiently, until the first beginnings of the light begin to appear.” The light appears not when we force it, but when we give ourselves room for the mind to drift.

Neuroscientists have a name for the brain’s wandering state: the default mode network. When we are not focused on an external task, this network becomes active, linking distant regions of the brain and allowing us to make associations that focused attention would never permit. It is the network of autobiographical memory, of perspective-taking, of creative synthesis. Some studies suggest that when people are allowed to daydream, they become better at solving problems that require insight. They can think more flexibly. They can see patterns. In other words, wandering is not a luxury; it is a cognitive necessity. A mind that is always on task is a mind that has lost the ability to connect.

This is true not only in the quiet space of our heads but also in the physical world. The act of walking has always been bound up with thinking. The Greek peripatetics walked while they taught. Rousseau said he could only meditate while walking. Thoreau traveled widely in Concord’s woods. Wordsworth composed poetry in motion, and his sister Dorothy recorded their rambles in journals that read like maps of an inner life. There is something about the rhythm of footsteps, the alternation of left and right, the steady breathing, that loosens the grip of linear thought. When we walk, the body moves through space, and the mind follows. You cannot force an insight by speed. But you can create the conditions for one.

The Situationists called this practice the dérive, or “drift.” They proposed that the city could be experienced not as a grid of functional destinations but as a territory of atmosphere and possibility. In a dérive, you let your attention be drawn by the mood of the streets, by the pull of a neighborhood, by the quietness of a courtyard, by the sound of traffic, by the strange light on a façade. You wander without a goal, and in doing so you discover the hidden psychogeography of the place—the subtle currents of feeling that official maps never record. The city becomes a text with many meanings, and you are its reader. This is not an act of escape from the world; it is an act of intimacy with it. To wander is to notice things that the purposeful traveler overlooks: the way a crack in the pavement becomes a river after rain, the way a row of shops can tell the story of a hundred years, the way a stranger’s laughter in a café seems to belong to some larger story you will never know.

In literature, wandering is almost the root of narrative itself. Odysseus did not want to wander. He wanted to get home. But his journey was shaped by storms and monsters and gods, by dalliances and detours, by everything that pushed him off course. And yet the Odyssey is not about the straight line from Troy to Ithaca. It is about the ten years of wandering in between, because it is there that the hero is tested, humbled, and transformed. Don Quixote wanders through La Mancha, mistaking windmills for giants, pursuing a vision that the world refuses to honor. His wanderings are absurd and beautiful, a rebuke to the idea that a life must be sensible and efficient. Even the hobbits in The Lord of the Rings begin with a home and a plan of sorts, but they are continually diverted, lost, and re-routed, and it is precisely those diversions that make them who they are. The path of the hero is never a straight line. It is a spiral, a meander, a series of wrong turns that turn out to be right.

Perhaps that is why the image of the journey is so universal. We tell our lives as stories, and stories require detours. A life narrated as a simple itinerary—“I was born, I worked, I died”—is hardly a story at all. What makes a story worth telling is the unexpected, the mistake that became a blessing, the road not taken that was taken anyway, the encounter with a stranger that changed everything. When we wander, we write the first drafts of our own plots. We give ourselves the gift of contingency. And in a world that increasingly tries to predict what we will do and want and think, contingency is a kind of freedom.

The ethics of wandering go beyond the personal. To wander is to be open to what is different from us—to other people, other places, other ways of being. A tourist with an itinerary sees what they have already seen in a brochure. A wanderer meets the unexpected: a festival in a small square, a conversation that begins with a lost direction, a meal that cannot be named. The wanderer learns to trust the world a little more, to accept that not everything can be controlled. This is a form of humility. It is also a form of courage. We live in a culture that values mastery, certainty, and control. Wandering asks us to relinquish those things, at least for a while. It asks us to be comfortable with not knowing. And that discomfort can be generative, because it forces us to rely on our senses, our instincts, and our capacity for wonder.

This does not mean we should renounce all goals. That would be another kind of rigidity. Rather, it means we should hold our goals lightly, and allow ourselves the freedom to be wrong. The artist who sets out to paint a masterpiece usually fails; the artist who sets out to explore a color or a shape sometimes succeeds. The scientist who conducts an experiment with a fixed expectation may overlook the anomaly; the scientist who is curious about what will happen may discover something new. The entrepreneur who is obsessed with a five-year plan may miss the opportunity that appears in the margins. Wandering is not the opposite of purpose. It is the companion of purpose—the part that keeps purpose alive by letting it breathe.

In practical terms, we can cultivate wandering in small ways. We can leave our phones behind for an afternoon. We can take a walk with no destination, letting our legs decide. We can allow ourselves to be bored without immediately reaching for a screen. We can read an article by an author we know nothing about. We can sit in a café and watch people, inventing stories for them. We can follow a curiosity that has no obvious payoff. These are not grand acts. They are almost embarrassingly simple. But they are also acts of resistance against the machinery of attention that wants to keep us in our lanes. They remind us that we are not just consumers of experience; we are creators of it. And they teach us that time is not only a resource to be measured and spent—it is a medium for living.

A friend of mine once decided to spend a summer wandering her own city. She was new to the place, had no job, no commitments. Every morning she chose a direction at random—north, south, east, west—and walked until she felt she had reached the edge of her curiosity. Then she came home and wrote about what she had seen. By the end of the summer, she knew the city better than people who had lived there for decades. She knew the best bakeries, the hidden gardens, the alleys where the cats congregated. But more than that, she knew herself. She had learned how to be alone with her thoughts, how to be open to chance, how to find beauty in the ordinary. Her wandering had not been wasted time. It had been a course in attention.

There is a saying that the map is not the territory. We carry maps everywhere now: digital maps that reroute us around traffic, algorithmically curated maps of news and culture, maps of our friendships built on likes and shares. These maps are useful. They save time. They prevent us from getting lost. But they can also prevent us from ever being lost, and being lost—temporarily, fruitfully lost—is one of the most instructive experiences a human being can have. When we are lost, we must look up. We must ask for help. We must notice the shape of the streets, the angle of the sun, the location of landmarks. We must use our intelligence and our intuition. And when we find our way again, we know something we did not know before: that we are capable of finding it. The same is true of the mind. We must sometimes allow ourselves to be lost in thought, to lose the thread of the argument, to forget what we were looking for, because in that forgetting we may find something better.

Wandering is also a way of honoring the complexity of time. Modern culture treats time as a commodity: we budget it, we track it, we fear wasting it. But time is not simply a quantity. It has texture and depth. An hour spent staring at a screen can feel like an instant and yet leave us empty. An hour spent wandering can feel like an eternity and yet leave us refreshed. To wander is to refuse the tyranny of the clock, to experience time as the Greeks conceived it—not as chronos, the measurable ticking of one thing after another, but as kairos, the opportune moment, the fullness of time. When we wander, we are not killing time. We are filling it with presence. We are making it unforgettable.

There will always be reasons not to wander: deadlines, obligations, responsibilities, fears. We cannot all abandon our lives and hike into the mountains. But we can all make space for wandering, even in small pockets. We can take a different route home and notice the houses with painted doors. We can let our thoughts drift instead of forcing them into a bullet-point list. We can start a conversation with a stranger and see where it goes. We can read a poem we don’t understand. We can look at the sky for no reason. These are not forms of procrastination. They are forms of enrichment. They remind us that the world is larger than our plans, that the self is deeper than our tasks, that life is not a problem to be solved but a mystery to be experienced.

The French poet Charles Baudelaire had a term for the wandering observer: the flâneur. The flâneur strolls through the arcades and boulevards of Paris, idly watching, listening, absorbing. He seems unproductive. He buys nothing, does nothing, goes nowhere. But in his aimlessness, he sees what the busy pedestrian cannot: the patterns of the city, the faces of the crowd, the flickering of light and shadow. Baudelaire understood that the flâneur is not a loafer but a kind of philosopher, a poet of the streets, a detective of the everyday. His wandering is not absence—it is attention.

In the end, wandering is a posture toward life. It is the willingness to say yes to the detour, to accept the wrong turn, to trust that the unknown holds something for us. It is the belief that meaning is not only found at the destination but also made in the movement, in the choices and accidents that shape the way. We are all, whether we admit it or not, on a journey we do not fully understand. None of us knows what will happen next year, next week, tomorrow. We think we are in control, but we are not. We are wanderers in a world of infinite paths, and the only real map is the one we draw with our footsteps, our thoughts, our loves, our memories.

So let us wander while there is still time. Let us leave the familiar road and follow the path that has no name. Let us be lost enough to be found. The destination will still be there. It will not mind waiting. It is the journey that matters, and the journey is made of detours.

### A Field Guide to Small Things

There is a jar of basil cuttings on my kitchen counter, a rough Mason jar with water cloudy from neglect. The cuttings have been there for three weeks. I meant to plant them. The roots have finally grown into a soft white tangle, a small underwater forest that shifts whenever I refill the water. I have not planted them because I like the jar. I like how it turns a bright green growing thing into a strange suspended structure, roots like veins, stems like veins, a whole body of translucent in-between. I like how small it is. It asks for almost nothing, and I give it almost nothing, and still it makes roots.

I have been trying to learn how to be alive to small things. That sounds like something a self-help book would say, and I apologize. But I mean something less tidy. I mean the discipline of looking at a jar of basil for long enough that the looking becomes a kind of holding. I mean the way a cloud of roots can pull your attention out of the factory of your own head and give it back to you, cleaner, the way a tide returns a piece of glass that has been rolled and rolled until it is no longer sharp.

We live most of our lives at dashboard level. We scan the instrument cluster of our days: the red lights, the alerts, the unread counts, the temperature warnings, the fuel gauge, the little icons for Bluetooth and battery and weather. I am as guilty as anyone. I check my phone perhaps four hundred times a day, and I am not proud of that number; I only half-remember reading it in a study and then the number became its own tiny obsidian idol. I check it even when I don’t need to. I check it as if checking is a physical tic, a nervous twitch of the soul. The strange thing is that I have almost nothing urgent waiting for me. The infinite scroll is not the problem, and the problem is not the technology either. The problem is the attention itself, or what we let happen to it: we trade it, a few coins at a time, for pieces of what other people had for breakfast, for arguments with strangers who are not even arguing with us, for a series of little jolts that leave us tired but somehow also underfed.

My grandfather had a workshop at the back of his house, and the smell of it was sawdust, machine oil, and something like dried sweat. He fixed lamps and lawnmower engines, radios with cracked Bakelite cases, old coffee grinders, a grandfather clock that never kept time. I used to sit on the overturned milk crate and watch him do nothing. That is what I remember. The nothing. He would hold a bolt between his thumb and forefinger and look at it for a long time, as if the bolt might tell him where it belonged. He would turn a piece of metal over in his hand and read it the way another man might read a newspaper. Once, I asked him how he knew what was wrong with something. He said, “Because I listen to it.” I thought he was being silly. A lamp doesn’t make a sound. But he meant a different kind of listening. He meant paying attention to the details until they began to form the shape of the answer. He meant spending an afternoon on a single drill bit because the job deserves the job.

He died when I was thirteen, and I inherited a tool chest full of random things: screws sorted by no discernible logic, washers in a Tobacco tin, springs looking like tiny coiled snakes, a set of jeweler’s screwdrivers whose handles had the warm turning color of old bone. I don’t know how to fix anything. But I have kept the chest. I think I kept it as a reminder that there was once a kind of attention that did not need to be captured. It simply gave itself over, freely, like water taking the shape of a cup. I am not like that. My attention is a dog that runs off and comes back only when I have something to eat. But I am training it.

This is not a new complaint. People have been mourning their attention spans since the invention of the novel, or the pocket watch, or the alphabet. I know that. I know I am not special. But I also know that something about the current arrangement feels different in degree so vast that it becomes a difference in kind. The dashboard never dims. The alerts are designed by thousands of smart people in rooms full of beanbags and complicated coffee machines, and they are designed to feel like being needed. They are designed to make you worry. I worry, and then I check, and the checking settles the worry for about thirty seconds, and then the worry returns with a new shape, a new hunger. It is a machine for generating the sensation of being useful without ever being useful.

Meanwhile, the basil roots are growing. That is the important part. They are growing in water, in a jar, in a room where I live, and they do not care one bit about my productivity. They do not care about the email I have not answered or the article I have not finished. They do not care that I am behind on everything, that my to-do list stretches around the block and down the street and into a neighboring state. They are making roots, which is what they have always done, and will do, and they do it at their own pace. I find this almost unbearably moving. The basil is not trying to be anything. It is not shooting for its potential. It is not practicing gratitude or manifesting abundance. It is just being basil, and because it is being basil, it is doing the only holy thing it can do.

I have begun to take walks without an object. Or rather, with a different kind of object: not to get somewhere, not to be seen, not to rack up steps, but to see. I live in a city, so there is plenty to see if you are willing to look slowly. There is a man who waters the same patch of pavement outside his apartment every evening with a red watering can. There is a crack in the sidewalk that has become a delta system, braided and branching, and a tiny oak tree has taken root in it. The oak is about a foot high. It will probably be pulled out, or stepped on, or dried out, but for now it is a complete tree, made to scale, a bonsai of persistence. There is a coffee shop with a sign in the window that has said “Back in 5 minutes” for at least a year. There is a blue door I have never noticed before, even though I have walked past it a hundred times, and now I cannot unsee it. It is the blue of old toys, of my mother’s bathtub, of a certain kind of sky before dusk. It has a brass knocker shaped like a lion’s head, and the lion’s eyes are worn smooth as if by the touch of a million thumbs. But I am the one who touched it. I did. I walked up to the door and put my thumb on the lion’s eyes. I looked around afterward, embarrassed, but no one was watching. Everyone was looking at their own dashboard.

There is a word for this kind of walking. The French call it *flânerie*, but the word is too dressed up, too literary. I prefer the old Welsh word *cwtch*, which means both a cuddle and a small, hidden space. Or the Japanese *shinrin-yoku*, forest bathing, though I am urban and my bath is of concrete. Maybe there is a word in some language for the act of paying attention to the small, specific, useless particulars of being alive, and if there is, I want to live in that word. If there isn’t, I want to invent it. Let’s call it *the discipline of the blue door*. Every walk is an exercise in the discipline. Every street becomes a field guide. Every man with a watering can becomes a page. This is what my grandfather was doing in his workshop, I realize now. He was not fixing lamps. He was practicing a discipline. The lamp was just an excuse to have something to hold.

The strange thing is that when I pay attention, time changes. It stretches. A fifteen-minute walk can feel like an hour. A single basil cutting can hold an afternoon. Time is supposed to be money, but attention is the opposite: it spends and yet produces no wealth, or produces a different kind of wealth that has no price and cannot be displayed, and so we are told it is worthless. But what if worth is the wrong metric entirely? What if the point is not value but intimacy? What if the point is to be, for one small part of one small day, completely inside the present tense, like a root in water, like a thumb on a lion’s eye, like a man reading a bolt?

I have a friend who is a nurse, and she once told me that the dying do not ask for more time. They ask for meaning, for forgiveness, for the face of someone they love. And they often ask for water. Not for water in the abstract, but for a specific glass of water, a sip that tastes like a sip. She said that in her thirty years of working in hospice she never once heard someone say, “I wish I had checked my email more.” She did hear someone say, “I wish I had noticed the way the rain made the roses smell.” She heard a man who had been an engineer his whole life say that his greatest accomplishment was not a bridge but the apple tree he had planted outside his bedroom window. It had taken him forty years to realize it. The tree had been growing the whole time.

I think about that man a lot. Forty years. The tree was growing while he was at work, while he was earning promotions, while he was checking his watch, while he was doing the things that he thought were the things. And then one day he was dying, and the tree was outside his window, and it was the most important thing he had ever made. He didn’t make the tree exactly. He planted it. He watered it. He paid attention to it. That is the difference. He participated in its becoming, and the participation took almost no time at all. A hole, a sapling, a few buckets of water, a lifetime of looking up from the dashboard. That is all.

There is a concept in Celtic Christianity called “thin places,” places where the veil between the visible and the invisible is worn thin. I used to think those places were geographical, like the ruins of an island monastery or a hilltop with no trees. But I have begun to believe that thin places are not places at all. They are acts of attention. A thin place is a moment when you look at a basil root and see the entire architecture of life. A thin place is when the blue door becomes more real than the email. A thin place is when the man with the watering can is not a stranger but a fellow creature, holy in his pointless chore. The veil is always thin. We are the ones who are thick. We are the ones who have become insulated, dashboarded, wrapped in our own busyness. We are the ones who have made the veil thick with our own resistance.

I have been trying to practice resistance by doing almost nothing. I take a chair out to the small balcony and sit. I do not look at my phone. I do not listen to a podcast. I do not “use” the time for reflection or mindfulness or journaling. I just sit, the way my grandfather sat in his workshop, and I let the world come to me. At first it is terrible. My brain screams for stimulation. It wants the jolt. It is like a caffeine headache that will not stop. But after ten minutes, something softens. The traffic noise stops being noise and becomes a pattern. The motor hum of a refrigerator becomes a kind of chant. A pigeon lands on the railing. The pigeon is absurd. It bobs its head like a metronome. It eyes a stale crust of bread. I watch it for a long time. I watch it see the bread. I watch it decide. It walks around the bread, considers, pecks. It carries the bread away. I have never seen such a complete story.

Attention is not the same as love, but it is the root of it. You cannot love what you do not notice. You cannot care for what you do not see. And I wonder if the real crisis of our time is not loneliness or anxiety or polarization or any of the other words we use to describe the weather of our lives, but something more fundamental: the collapse of the faculty of wonder. We are losing the ability to be amazed by the ordinary. And if we lose that, we lose everything, because everything is ordinary. Everything. The birth of a child is an ordinary miracle; it happens at varying statistical rates in hospitals and homes around the world. The turning of the Earth is ordinary. The rise of a loaf of bread is a once-in-a-lifetime miracle that occurs three times a week in everyone’s kitchen. And the only way to see the miracle is to pay attention to it. To see it as if for the first time. To see it as if it were a blue door that was always there but you somehow never noticed.

I have been trying to write this piece, and I realize I have not once mentioned the basil since the beginning except to say it is still there. Let me check. Yes, it is still there. The water is cloudier, the roots are longer, and a new leaf has opened, a bright pale green, almost translucent at first, like a wing before it hardens. I have not planted the basil, and I think I never will. It has become a lesson. A few cuttings in a jar of water can sustain themselves for weeks, months even, as long as they have light and a little attention. They are not growing toward anything but more roots, more leaves, more basil. They are not trying to become a tomato plant. They are not envious of the spider plant on the shelf. They are completely, utterly themselves. That, I think, is the hardest thing in the world. Not to be extraordinary. To be ordinary. To be a person who is late, who is forgetful, who has a jar of basil cuttings on the counter and no plan to plant them, who takes walks and looks at blue doors, who sits on a balcony and watches a pigeon, and who calls that attendance. To be ordinary is to be accounted for, not in the ledgers of productivity, but in the small ongoing account of the world.

My grandfather’s workshop was a thin place. I see it now. The workbench was an altar. The topless tin of nails was a reliquary. The drill bits were saints. He was not a religious man, but he was deeply reverent, and his reverence was a matter of attention. He would not have explained it that way. If you had asked him about a lamp, he would have said, “It’s got a loose wire.” But that was a translation. The wire was not the problem. The problem was that the lamp had been neglected, that no one had looked at it closely enough, that the attention had broken. The lamp was a great teacher of attention disguised as a household object.

I am trying to be like that. I am trying to be a great teacher of attention disguised as nothing special. The basil jar teaches attention. The blue door teaches attention. The pigeon teaches attention, accidentally, by being exactly what it is. I want to be exactly what I am. But what am I? I am a person who gets distracted, who checks the phone, who loses the thread, who forgets. I am a person who sometimes looks up and sees the light falling on a wall and thinks, *that is enough*. I am a person who sometimes sits so long that the quiet begins to glow. And then I ruin it by thinking about how quiet it is, and then I am no longer in the quiet but talking about it, and that is the comedy and the tragedy and the whole business of being alive.

I have no grand conclusion. I have only the jar of basil. I am going to go look at it now. The roots will have grown a fraction of a fraction further. The water will be slightly cloudier. A leaf will have turned toward the window. The afternoon will have advanced. I will have missed a text. I will have lost nothing. I will have gained a moment that cannot be downloaded, cannot be liked, cannot be captured, cannot be sold. It will be mine only in the way a root is a root, only in the way a blue door is a blue door, only in the way a glass of water is a glass of water. That is enough. That is everything. That is the practice. I think my grandfather would have liked that. I think he would have grunted, which was his way of saying yes.

There is a jar of basil cuttings on my kitchen counter. I meant to plant them. I have not, and I will not. They are not supposed to be anywhere else. They are exactly where they belong, in water, in light, in a room where someone is trying, imperfectly, to pay attention. That is the only work. That is the whole work.

# In Praise of Wandering

There is a particular pleasure in walking down a street you have never seen before. Not with the purpose of reaching a monument or a well-reviewed café, but simply walking, letting the world unfold at its own pace. I remember doing this as a child: leaving the house with no firm plan, following the sidewalk until it turned to gravel, then to a dirt path, then to a field. The world seemed enormous because I was willing to get lost. Somewhere along that path I learned something that formal education later tried to teach out of me: that the most valuable discoveries are made when you are not looking for anything in particular.

Wandering is perhaps the oldest human way of thinking. Before we had maps, we had stories; before we had destinations, we had curiosity. To wander is to allow the world to ask a question of you, rather than forcing the world to answer yours. Our age, however, is not kind to wandering. We optimize our commutes, schedule our weekends, measure our steps and our screen time. Every app asks what we are looking for. The idea of moving through space—or through thought—without a goal can feel almost immoral, like wasting time. But time spent wandering is never wasted. It is the soil out of which meaning grows.

Consider walking. Not the purposeful power-walk of someone trying to get in their ten thousand steps, but the slow, open-ended stroll of someone who has nowhere to be. There is a reason the French have the word *flâneur*, a man who saunters around observing society, and it is not because they wanted an excuse to be lazy. The flâneur is a kind of philosopher, reading the city as if it were a book. In every shop window, every face, every half-heard conversation, there is a story. The wanderer notices a small crack in a wall where a vine has taken root. He sees an old woman feeding pigeons in a square that no one else seems to use. He hears a busker playing a song he has never heard, and for a moment the whole street stops to listen. None of this appears in any itinerary. None of it can be Googled. It can only be encountered.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who did some of his best thinking while walking in the countryside, wrote: “I can only meditate when I am walking. When I stop, I cease to think; my mind only works with my legs.” Many great thinkers have felt the same. The philosopher Søren Kierkegaard took long walks through Copenhagen, dashing back to his desk to write what had come to him. Henry David Thoreau walked several hours a day, insisting that “the moment my legs begin to move, my thoughts begin to flow.” This is not a coincidence. There is a rhythm to walking—the swing of the arms, the steady pulse of the feet—that seems to unlock something in the mind. It is as if the body, while moving through space, gives the mind permission to move through time: backward into memory, forward into possibility, sideways into association.

Neuroscientists have begun to explain what the poets always knew. When we are not focused on a task, the brain enters something called the default mode network. This is the network that lights up when we daydream, when we stare out a window, when our attention drifts. It is the network associated with creativity, with making connections between distant ideas, with imagining alternative futures. In other words, the brain is never really idle. When we think we are doing nothing, we are actually doing something profound. We are wandering through our own mental landscapes, and that wandering is what allows us to solve problems that resistance to focused thought cannot crack.

How many of us have had a brilliant idea in the shower? How many have found the answer to a stubborn problem while out for a run? The insight appears as if from nowhere, but it was not nowhere. It was the result of a long process of incubation, one that required periods of relaxation and openness. The creative mind works by alternating between focus and diffuse attention. A problem is attacked directly for a while, then abandoned. The unconscious keeps chewing on it. And then, at the most unexpected moment, the solution appears. Archimedes did not discover his principle while He was seated at a desk. He was in a bath, relaxing, and the water spilled over the edge. Newton did not formulate the law of gravity while laboriously calculating orbits. He was sitting under a tree, watching an apple fall. Whether or not these stories are literally true, they capture an important truth: the greatest breakthroughs often arrive at the edges of consciousness, in the margins of purposeful effort.

Wandering, then, is not the opposite of thinking. It is a different kind of thinking, one that honors the mysterious way the mind actually works. It is a mode of attention that is less controlled but more alert. The poet William Wordsworth wrote that poetry “takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity.” But tranquillity, for Wordsworth, was not passivity. It was a kind of walking meditation. He composed many of his most famous poems while striding through the Lake District, muttering to himself, pausing to look at a flower or a cloud. The landscape was not just a backdrop for his poetry; it was a participant in it. The hills, the waters, the sheep, the ruined abbeys—these were the elements out of which he built his inner world.

There is a reason that so many spiritual traditions use the image of the path. The pilgrim has no illusions that the road is comfortable. The road is where the soul is tested and transformed. In Dante’s *Divine Comedy*, the poem begins with a man who, halfway through his life, finds himself lost in a dark wood. The whole of his journey—through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise—is a wandering guided by love and grace. He does not know where each step will lead. He must trust the road. Similarly, the ancient Greek hero Odysseus does not sail directly home from Troy. He wanders for ten years, encountering cyclopes, sirens, witches, and the land of the dead. His journey is a circle, but within that circle is the entire ocean of human experience. The *Odyssey* is the first great western novel precisely because it understands that the detour is the story. If Odysseus had gone straight home, there would be no epic. There would only be a weather report.

Narrative itself is a kind of wandering. A story begins with a disruption—a village burned, a letter delivered, a stranger walking into town—and then it follows the protagonist as she wanders in search of a solution. The middle of a story is full of unpredictable roads, false leads, and sudden discoveries. The reader, like the protagonist, does not know what will happen next. That uncertainty is the engine of meaning. We do not read stories to know the ending. We read them to dwell in the middle, to wander through the details of another life. A good book is not a bullet train to a conclusion. It is a labyrinth, and the pleasure is in getting lost.

Wandering also shapes the way we know places. There is a huge difference between visiting a city as a tourist, following a map from one famous landmark to another, and walking into a neighborhood where no one has told you to go. In the first case, the city is a sequence of pictures, already familiar from postcards. In the second, the city becomes three-dimensional, smells and sounds, textures and moods. You might turn a corner and find a bakery that has been there for eighty years. You might sit on a bench and watch a group of children playing soccer in the rain. You might get caught in an unexpected shower and duck into a doorway where you meet a retired violin maker who tells you his whole life story. None of this is efficient. But it is alive.

The twentieth-century movement known as psychogeography understood this deeply. The Situationists, led by Guy Debord, proposed a practice called the *dérive*—a drift through the urban landscape, guided by nothing but the feelings and encounters that arise along the way. Instead of treating the city as a set of routes to be navigated, the dérive treated it as a vast emotional terrain, full of currents and eddies. The goal was not to get somewhere. The goal was to let the city reveal itself, to become aware of the atmospheres and histories that official maps could not capture. For Debord, walking was a form of resistance. To drift was to refuse the logic of productivity, to reclaim the city as a space of play and wonder rather than commerce and traffic.

The idea of wandering as resistance resonates now more than ever. We live in a culture obsessed with optimization. Our language is full of words like *efficiency*, *deliverables*, *targets*, *scalability*. Social media encourages us to present our lives as a linear sequence of achievements. We are constantly told to be more productive, to read more books, to learn more skills, to monetize our hobbies. In such a culture, the simple act of wandering—of walking without a destination, of daydreaming, of following a whim—is almost subversive. It says: I am not a machine. I am not a resource to be optimized. I am a creature who is curious about the world. And curiosity, by definition, does not know what it is looking for. If it knew, it would no longer be curiosity.

Of course, not all wandering is leisurely. There is a kind of wandering that comes from displacement—the refugee who wanders because home is no longer safe, the exile who wanders because the borders of the world have closed around her. This is the dark side of wandering, the side we must never romanticize away. To wander unwillingly, without food or hope, is not freedom. It is suffering. We must be careful not to confuse the voluntary wandering of the flâneur with the forced wandering of the displaced. The first is a privilege; the second is a wound. But perhaps it is precisely this wound that has produced some of the most powerful art of our time. Exile, as many writers have noted, sharpens the memory. The person who has lost a homeland sees it more vividly than the person who has never left. The refugee's wandering is a kind of testimony, a remembering of what has been lost. And in that remembering, the wandering mind finds meaning.

Wandering through time is just as important as wandering through space. Memory is a strange, meandering path. We think we remember an event, but what we actually remember is the last time we remembered it. Each recollection is a new visit to an old place, and the place has changed. The French writer Marcel Proust built a two-thousand-page novel out of a single act of wandering memory. In *In Search of Lost Time*, the narrator tastes a madeleine dipped in tea, and suddenly the entire world of his childhood, with its church steeples and summer afternoons, floods into his mind. He does not follow a straight line. He follows scent, taste, emotion. The novel is a web of digressions, a endless wandering through time, and it is precisely this wandering that makes it feel true. Our own lives are not neatly chronological. They are made of moments, fragments, associations. When we let our minds wander, we are not wasting time. We are tracing the actual shape of our lives.

The same is true of the future. We often imagine that we should have a five-year plan, a clear map of where we are going. But nobody actually gets to a great life by following a blueprint. They arrive, as the novelist William Gibson put it, through a series of improvisations and accidents. The career you end up loving is the one you discovered by chance. The friendship that sustains you begins with a random conversation. The book that changes you is the one you picked up because you liked the cover. This is not a plea for chaos. It is a plea for openness. The future, like a landscape, is too vast to be mapped in advance. The best we can do is have a compass, a vague sense of direction, and the courage to wander.

In the Middle Ages, before the printing press, scholars used a word for the act of reading: *legere*. It meant to gather, to select, to wander among the texts. A reader was not a passive consumer. She was a wanderer, moving from one insight to another, making her own path through the forest of words. When we read today, we often want everything immediately: summaries, key takeaways, five bullet points. But the richness of reading lies in the detours, in the passages that have nothing to do with the thesis, in the long descriptions of weather and landscape and clothing that seem irrelevant until they become unforgettable. Literature is an invitation to wander. To read closely is to walk slowly.

There is also a sacred dimension to wandering. The pilgrimage, as old as humanity, is a journey to a holy place. But the real holiness lies not in the destination but in the walking itself. The medieval pilgrims who walked from Chartres to Santiago de Compostela did not simply want to arrive. They wanted to be changed by the road. They sought hunger, fatigue, the open sky, the encounter with strangers. They carried few things, because the journey required them to let go. The tradition of the *wanderer* runs through every religion: the Buddha leaving his palace to walk the dusty roads of India, Jesus wandering through Galilee with nowhere to lay his head, the Sufi dervishes who traveled as a form of prayer. Wandering is not a retreat from the world. It is a way of being in the world, a way of paying attention to the mystery that surrounds us. Every step is a prayer. Every road is a revelation.

What does it mean to dwell? Martin Heidegger wrote that the essence of human life is “dwelling.” But dwelling, for him, did not mean owning a house. It meant belonging—being rooted, being attuned to the place where you live. How do we come to dwell in a place? Not by buying property, but by knowing the place intimately. And the only way to know a place intimately is to wander through it, again and again, letting it become part of your body. The wanderer knows where the sun rises on the plaza, where the first leaves fall in autumn, which café has the strong coffee and which has the good conversation. To dwell is to have a relationship with a place, and relationships require time. They require wandering hand in hand through the ordinary days. The city that you have wandered through is a city you will never forget. It has become a part of your internal landscape.

I have noticed that my own best thoughts do not come at the desk. They come while I am washing the dishes, folding laundry, walking to the store, staring at the sky. They come when I'm not trying to think. The moment I try to seize them, they vanish. The mind is like a small animal that approaches only when you are still and quiet. If you chase it, it runs. But if you sit, or walk, and let your thoughts drift, it comes and sits beside you. This is the wisdom of the wanderer: nothing of importance can be forced. Our greatest insights are given to us, not produced. We can prepare the ground, and then we must wait. The waiting is not passivity. It is a kind of active openness, a wandering through the fields of the possible.

The universal experience of taking a shower and suddenly solving the problem you have been wrestling with for days is a perfect image of this. The water is warm, the mind is unoccupied, and for a few moments you are not trying to be anywhere. You are somewhere within yourself. The answer appears, not because you demanded it, but because you let it. There is a Spanish proverb that says: *Hitch your wagon to a star, but take the longest road*—perhaps because the longest road is the one that offers the most chances for transformation. If we always take the straightest line, we will miss everything that lies between our origin and our destination. And what lies between is most of life.

We need to reclaim the right to wander. We need to be unembarrassed about taking a walk for no reason, about staring out the window, about letting a Sunday afternoon dissolve into nothing. We need to remember that the best conversations are the ones that ramble, that one topic leads to another, and we end up somewhere we never expected. We need to allow our children to get bored, because boredom is the beginning of creativity. A child who is bored must invent, must wander, must find something that does not exist yet. The child who is scheduled from morning to night never learns to listen to the inner voice. The inner voice speaks quietly, and it speaks in a way that is not linear. It takes detours. It follows fragments. It changes its mind. It needs room.

In the end, wandering is not about going nowhere. It is about going somewhere without knowing where that is. It is an act of trust in the unknown. The world is vast and full of beauty, but we will not see it from the highway. We will see it from the side roads, the footpaths, the alleys that no guidebook mentions. We will see it when we are willing to get lost. Getting lost is how we find things—not the things we thought we were looking for, but the things that we did not know we needed. It is how we find ourselves.

So wander. Wander with your feet and with your mind. Wander in the garden, in the library, in the long memory of the night. Wander through the neighborhoods of your own heart. Do not ask where you will end up. Ask what you will notice along the way. The universe is not a checkpoint; it is a cloud, shimmering with possibility. Every step is a sentence in a story you cannot yet read. Every corner is a door. Every road asks the same question, the oldest question in the world: *What do you see?* And the only answer worth giving, from a wanderer, is: *I don't know yet. Let me look.*

The Permission to Notice

There is a particular kind of quiet that exists only on a weekday afternoon in a small city, when most people are indoors doing whatever it is that people do, and the streets belong to the old, the very young, and the unemployable. I found myself in that quiet once, not by choice but by circumstance, sitting on a bench outside a post office with nothing to do and nowhere to be. I had no phone. I had no book. I had only the afternoon, and the strange, uncomfortable gift of being unoccupied.

At first it felt like a kind of poverty. I watched a pigeon walk a circle around a discarded sandwich wrapper, its head bobbing with that mechanical certainty pigeons have, as if they are always nodding at an invisible metronome. I watched a woman emerge from the post office with a cardboard tube under her arm, glance at the sky, and then walk left, out of my life forever. I watched a cloud move across the sun and change the temperature of my own skin by a degree. None of this mattered. None of this would make a difference in any ledger of achievement. And yet, sitting there, I began to feel something I had almost forgotten: the texture of being present.

We live in an age of constant interruption, but more than that, we live in an age of constant invitation. Every device in our pocket is a door to somewhere else, and we walk through those doors thousands of times a day, so often that we forget we are walking anywhere at all. We flit from one small screen to the next like a dragonfly skimming a pond, touching the surface of a thousand things but never sinking into any of them. The result is a peculiar kind of exhaustion, not from doing too much, but from being nowhere fully. We are always almost somewhere else. The present moment becomes a waiting room, and the only escape is the next notification, the next scroll, the next small hit of novelty.

I have been thinking about attention lately, not as a skill or a productivity hack, but as a form of love. To pay attention to something is to say, with your whole body, that it matters. When you really look at a leaf, you are not merely registering its shape and color; you are entering into a relationship with it. You are giving it your time, and time is the only currency we truly have. The leaf, of course, does not know or care. But you are changed by the looking. The act of attention is a kind of hospitality, an offering of the self to the world, and in that offering, you receive the world back, not as a series of data points, but as a presence.

I used to walk the same route to work every day, and I could not have told you a single thing about it. The route took me past a bakery, a park, a row of brownstones, and a construction site. I was in my head, rehearsing conversations, composing emails, worrying about the future, rewriting the past. The physical world was a blur at the edge of a mental movie. Then one day, a friend told me about a practice she called “the first ten minutes,” in which she forced herself, every morning, to walk the route without any internal narration. No planning, no judging, no commentary. Just the sensation of walking. The first time she tried it, she said, she noticed that the bakery had a green awning, and that it had been there for years, and that she had never seen it. She noticed that the park had a particular smell, like damp earth and cut grass, and that the brownstones each had a different kind of door handle, some brass, some iron, some glass. She noticed that the construction site had a mural painted on its plywood fence, and the mural had a small, painted bird in the corner, and the bird looked like it was winking.

I tried her practice the next morning, and it was agonizing. My mind rebelled. It wanted to think. It wanted to plan. It wanted to be anywhere but here, in the ordinary world. But I kept at it, and after a week, something shifted. The world began to appear. Not all at once, but in fragments, like a photograph developing in a tray of chemicals. I noticed that the bakery had a green awning. I noticed the door handles. I noticed the bird. And I realized, with a kind of shock, that I had been walking through an extraordinary world and seeing almost none of it.

Attention is not just a matter of looking; it is a matter of being willing to be affected. There is a vulnerability in it. When you truly look at something, you cannot remain entirely separate from it. The boundary between self and world softens. The philosopher Simone Weil wrote that “attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” I think she meant that to give attention is to give your own inner life to something outside yourself, to suspend your own concerns long enough to let another thing be real. It is an act of self-emptying, and in a culture that tells us constantly to self-promote, to self-express, to self-optimize, self-emptying is almost countercultural.

I have found that attention can be trained, but not in the way we usually think of training. It is not about forcing yourself to concentrate harder, or enduring the boredom of a task until it becomes automatic. It is more like cultivating a habit of receptivity, a posture of openness. You cannot force yourself to notice things with the same determination you would use to lift a weight. You have to relax into noticing. You have to become, as the poet John Keats put it, a “negative capability,” a person capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason.

One of the best ways I know to do this is to walk without a destination. Not a power walk, not a hike with a goal at the end, but a ramble, a saunter, a stroll with no purpose other than to see. The word “saunter” is said to come from the Middle Ages, when pilgrims walked to the Holy Land, and people asked them where they were going. They would answer, “à la sainte terre,” to the holy land. Whether or not that etymology is true, I like to think of a walk as a pilgrimage to the only holy land that exists: the present moment. And when you walk that way, the world becomes a text, and you learn to read it.

I remember one autumn afternoon, during a period when I was deeply unhappy, I went for a walk in a neighborhood I had never visited. It was a residential area, unremarkable, with identical houses on identical streets. I was not expecting much. But as I walked, I began to notice that every house had a small detail that made it unique: a mailbox shaped like a barn, a wind chime made of seashells, a porch swing with a faded cushion, a garden gnome holding a tiny fishing rod. I became fascinated. I started to invent stories for each house. The barn mailbox belonged to a retired farmer who missed the Midwest. The seashell wind chime was hung by a woman who had never seen the ocean but dreamed of it. The porch swing was used every evening by a couple who had nothing to say to each other but liked sitting in silence together. The gnome with the fishing rod was a gift from a son who had died years ago, and now the gnome was all the family the old man had left. I knew, of course, that all these stories were false. But they were not meaningless. They were my way of paying attention, of giving each object the dignity of a story, of treating the world as if it were alive and full of meaning. And by the end of the walk, my unhappiness had not disappeared, but it had been put into perspective. I was not the only one with a story. Everyone and everything had one. I was part of a vast, interwoven narrative, and I had forgotten it.

There is a particular joy in noticing the small things that are easy to dismiss. I am thinking of the way light falls through a glass of water onto a white tablecloth, making a tiny, trembling rainbow. I am thinking of the sound of rain at different times of day, how it patters in the morning and drums at night. I am thinking of the way a spider web catches the dew, each droplet a tiny lens, the whole structure a piece of jewelry made by a blind artisan. To notice these things is to be rich in a way that cannot be taxed or taken away. They are not experiences you can have only once; they are recurring, endless, free. In a world that is always trying to sell you the next new thing, these small things are the oldest things, the eternal things, and they are waiting for you on every street corner, in every patch of grass, in every empty moment.

But attention is not always pleasant. To notice the world is also to notice its wounds. There is the plastic bag caught in the branches of a tree, which will be there for decades, a small monument to our carelessness. There is the crushed soda can on the sidewalk, the broken bottle, the graffiti that is not art but anger. There is the man sleeping on a bench in the park, and you notice that he has no socks, and you notice that it is October, and you notice that you have a home to go to and he does not. Attention is not a vacation. It is a willingness to be present to everything, the beautiful and the terrible. And if you are willing to be present to the terrible, you may be moved to act, to make a small difference, to offer a blanket or a dollar or just the recognition that he is a person, not a piece of the landscape.

I have come to believe that attention is also a form of resistance. The forces of distraction—the algorithms, the advertisers, the 24-hour news cycle—want you to be scattered, reactive, anxious, and numb. They want you to scroll past your own life. They want you to believe that the only meaningful moments are the ones you can photograph, share, and monetize. They want you to be always elsewher. To pay attention, relentlessly and joyfully, to the world in front of you is to refuse that bargain. It is to say: my life is here, not on your screen. It is to reclaim your own time, moment by moment, from the great, sucking vacuum of manufactured urgency. And it is to remember that the reality of the world is infinitely more complex, strange, and beautiful than anything the machine can feed you.

There is a practice in Zen Buddhism called “beginner’s mind.” It means approaching the world as if you are seeing it for the first time, without the filters of expectation or habit. I am not a Buddhist, but I have tried to cultivate this. I have tried to look at a coffee cup as if I had never seen one before: the smooth curve of the ceramic, the small chip on the rim, the way the steam rises in a spiral. I have tried to listen to a bird song without identifying the bird, hearing it purely as sound, a wild and intricate melody with no purpose but itself. I have tried to taste a piece of bread as if it were the first food I had ever eaten, noticing the sweetness of the crust, the soft crumb, the faint tang of salt. These experiments are hard. My mind wants to label, categorize, and move on. It wants to turn the coffee cup into the concept of a coffee cup and then stop seeing it. But when I can keep the beginner’s mind, even for a few minutes, the world becomes new again. I am no longer walking through a familiar landscape. I am walking through a miracle.

Time is strange when you pay attention. It does not pass in a uniform flow; it expands and contracts, deepens and thins. An hour spent scrolling through your phone can feel like five minutes, and afterward you cannot remember a single thing you saw. But five minutes spent watching a sunset can feel like an hour, and the memory of it can last a lifetime. Attention is the key to this mystery. When you are fully present, time slows down. It becomes thick, textured, rich. You are no longer a passive passenger, being carried toward the grave. You are an active participant, and every moment is a doorway into something larger than yourself. This is why children often seem to live in a different temporal world: they have not yet learned to rush. Everything is new to them, and so everything is worthy of attention. A puddle is a small ocean. A bug is a dragon. A cardboard box is a house. To recover this capacity is not to become childish, but to become wise.

I think of the writer and naturalist Henry David Thoreau, who built a cabin at Walden Pond and spent two years paying attention to the world around him. He wrote about the color of the ice, the flight of a hawk, the sound of a train in the distance. His book “Walden” is not really a book about nature; it is a book about attention. He went to the woods, he said, “to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach.” He did not need to travel to a distant country. The whole universe, he believed, was present in the rhythm of a single day, if you could only see it. For two years, an American writer paid attention, and out of that attention came a book that has touched millions of lives. The rest of us, perhaps, do not need to build a cabin. We need only to put down our phones and look out the window. We need only to take a walk without a destination. We need only to be willing to be bored, because in boredom the mind finally stops jumping and begins to settle, and when it settles, the world can appear.

But we are afraid of boredom. We have built an entire civilization to avoid it. We have invented endless forms of entertainment, distraction, and mere stimulation. We have made it possible to go from birth to death without ever being alone with our thoughts for a single moment. And yet boredom, paradoxically, is one of the most fertile states of mind. It is the fallow field. When we are bored, we are not doing anything, and in not doing anything, we open ourselves to the unexpected. The great aphorist and essayist Blaise Pascal wrote, “All of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.” He was not saying that we should never act. He was saying that we have lost the ability to be still, to be present, to pay attention, and from that stillness all true action should arise. The solution to our frenetic, anxious age is not more activity, more productivity, more input. It is the simple, radical act of sitting quietly in a room, and watching, and listening, and breathing.

I have been trying to do this, a little bit, every day. I sit in a chair by the window. I do not close my eyes or meditate in the formal sense. I just look. I see the neighbor’s cat climb the fence. I see the mailman walk his route. I see the clouds move, and the trees move in the wind, and the light change from yellow to gold to gray. Sometimes the minutes crawl. Sometimes they fly. But always, when I leave the chair, something has shifted. I am calmer. I am more connected. I remember that the world is real, that it exists independently of my worries, and that it is beautiful in a way that no screen can capture.

There is a poem by the British poet W.H. Auden called “Musée des Beaux Arts” about suffering and how it takes place “while someone else is eating or opening a window or just walking dully along.” He is talking about how the world ignores tragedy, but he is also, I think, pointing to the ordinariness of life as its greatest mystery. The miracles are not the spectacular ones; they are the everyday ones. The miracle of a child’s laugh. The miracle of a cup of hot tea on a cold morning. The miracle of a stranger’s smile. These are the things that sustain us, and we barely notice them. To pay attention is to see the miracle. To pay attention is to be alive.

In the end, that is what I want. Not to be successful or important or remembered, but to be alive, fully alive, to every moment that I am given. And I am learning that the way to be alive is to pay attention. To look. To listen. To taste. To touch. To be open, vulnerable, and willing to be affected by the world. The universe is indifferent, perhaps, but it is also astonishing. Every blade of grass is a testament to the improbability of existence. Every human face is a history of joy and sorrow. Every ordinary moment is a gift that will never come again. The least I can do is show up for it.

I sat on that bench outside the post office for a long time, watching the world go by. The pigeon finished its meal, the woman returned to her life, the cloud moved on. I did not have any great revelation. I did not solve any problem. But when I stood up to leave, I felt different. I had been somewhere. I had not been thinking about elsewhere. I had been here, and here had been enough.

That was a few years ago. I have not always lived up to the lesson of that afternoon. I have slipped back into the scrolling, the worrying, the chronic absent-mindedness. But the memory stays with me, a kind of beacon. And I know that I can return to that place whenever I choose, not the bench, but the state of mind. It is just a matter of attention. It is just a matter of deciding that what is right in front of me matters, and that I have the ability, and the privilege, to see it.

The writer Mary Oliver ended one of her poems with a question: “Tell me, what is it you plan to do / with your one wild and precious life?” I used to think that the answer had to be something grand: achieve, create, change the world. Now I think it might be simpler. I think the answer might be to pay attention, to live in wonder, to accept the world’s gifts with open hands, and to give them back with open eyes. The world is full of noise, but it is also full of silence, and in the silence, if we can find it, we hear the true heartbeat of things. That heartbeat is not made by us. But we can listen to it. We can be moved by it. We can carry it within us, and let it shape the way we walk through the days of our lives.

So write freely, you asked. This is what I want to write: that attention is the beginning of love, that presence is the beginning of peace, and that the ordinary world is holy ground. The bread is on the table. The light is on the floor. The bird is at the window. And because we are here, because we are conscious, because we can see and hear and feel, we are already participants in an astonishing mystery. Do not let it go unnoticed.
