samples.result:
# The Art of Wandering

I have been thinking lately about wandering—not the kind that requires a map, or a destination, or even a proper path, but the kind that happens when you put the map down and let the world take you by the elbow. It is an art, and like most arts, it has nearly disappeared from everyday life. We have become so good at moving from point A to point B, so efficient in our commutes and our schedules, that we have lost the ability to drift. We scroll, we swipe, we plan. We optimize. We measure our days in tasks completed, not in moments felt. But every now and then, if we are lucky, something breaks the rhythm—a sudden rain, a closed road, a forgotten appointment—and we find ourselves wandering again, not through space only, but through time and memory and attention. When that happens, I notice, the world looks different. It looks almost holy.

I remember a particular evening in late autumn. I was walking home through a neighborhood I knew well, the kind of neighborhood where every house has a lawn and every lawn has a sprinkler for the summer and a leaf pile for the fall. It was the hour before streetlights came on, when the sky turns the color of a bruise healing. I was not in a hurry, but I was not exactly present either. My mind was churning through the day’s small failures and the next day’s small tasks. Then something caught my eye: a crack in the sidewalk, spreading like a river delta. In that crack, a dandelion was growing. It was not a grand dandelion, not the kind you press into a book as a keepsake. It was stubborn, slightly yellowed, leaning as if it had been through a war. I stopped. I crouched. I looked at it for perhaps two minutes, which is a lifetime for a creature as restless as I usually am.

What struck me was not the dandelion itself, but the fact that I had passed this exact spot hundreds of times without ever seeing it. How many other things had I missed? How many small miracles had been performed in the margins of my vision while I stared at my phone or rehearsed conversations in my head? The dandelion was a kind of accusation. It asked me: what else are you not noticing? It was also an invitation. You could spend a whole life paying attention, it seemed to say, and still die unfinished.

That evening set me on a wandering course, not through any grand wilderness, but through the ordinary territories of my life. I began to walk without purpose. I began to look without expecting anything. I started to notice things I had been trained to ignore: the way light falls through a window at three in the afternoon, turning dust into gold; the particular weight of a doorknob when the house is empty; the sound of a refrigerator humming like a distant sea. These were not revelations in any dramatic sense. They were simply facts of existence, tiny and irreplaceable, waiting to be acknowledged. And the more I acknowledged them, the more the world seemed to thicken, to gain texture, to become something other than the flat backdrop of my ambitions.

There is a name for this, I learned later. The philosophers call it attention. William James wrote that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” He meant that reality is not a fixed thing, given to us whole, but a kind of allotment, parceled out by the focus of our minds. Two people can stand in the same room and live in entirely different worlds, depending on what they choose to see. The person who notices the dust motes in the sunbeam is not the same as the person who notices the crack in the wall, and neither is the same as the person who notices only the clock. Attention is not just a cognitive act. It is a moral act. It decides what counts. It decides what is real.

This is why the modern age is so troubling. We have more stimulation than any humans in history, yet we have less attention to give. Our devices are designed to capture us, to hold our gaze, to pull us toward the next notification with the precision of a fisherman’s hook. Every app is an engine of distraction. Every feed is a river of endless novelty. And in the middle of it, we sit, half-present, scrolling through other people’s lives while our own runs past us like a train we have forgotten to board. We are not wandering anymore. We are drifting, but not in the good way. We are drifting the way a plastic bag drifts across a parking lot—moved by every current, touching nothing, weighted by nothing.

The antidote, I think, is not to disconnect entirely. That is too simple, and too smug. The antidote is to reconnect with the local, the small, the particular. It is to walk down the same street a hundred times and try to see it as if for the first time. It is to sit with a cup of coffee and not reach for your phone, just to see what happens. It is to let your mind wander, not through a curated feed, but through the labyrinth of memory and desire and grief and wonder that you carry inside you. This kind of wandering is not passive. It is active. It requires courage. Because when you let your mind go where it wants to go, you will not always like the destination.

I tried this once, on a long bus ride through the countryside. I had no headphones. I had no book. I had only the window and the fields and the occasional farmhouse, and the strange, uncomfortable silence of my own skull. At first it was unbearable. I felt itchy, bored, almost panicked. My hand kept twitching toward my pocket. But I forced myself to stay. I watched the fences go by. I watched the cows lift their heads, one by one, as the bus roared past. I thought about a summer I spent at my grandmother’s house when I was nine years old, and how the hedges smelled of nettles and rain, and how she would kneel in her garden for hours, weeding, and I would kneel beside her, thinking she was moving too slowly. She told me once: “You have to know a plant before you can pull it up.” I thought she meant get close enough to see its leaves, but now I understand she meant something deeper. You have to know why it is there. You have to know what it is doing, what it is becoming, what it is holding in its roots. Only then can you decide if it belongs.

That bus ride became a kind of pilgrimage. Not because I was going anywhere sacred, but because I was returning to myself. Memory does that. It ambushes you. A smell, a sound, a particular quality of light, and suddenly you are not an adult on a bus; you are a child in a garden, and the world is enormous and tender and full of small things that matter. We spend so much of our lives trying to escape our memories, to outrun them, to curate them into something neat and presentable. But the memories that truly shape us are not neat. They are ragged. They are full of contradictions. They are like the dandelion in the crack, refusing to be pulled up, insisting on their place in the concrete.

I think that is why I have come to love the poetry of ordinary objects. A kitchen table, for instance. I once sat at a kitchen table in a house that was being emptied for an estate sale. The owners had died—an old couple, no children—and the furniture was being sold to strangers. I was there because I knew the family, and I wanted to pay my respects, but also because I was curious. What remains of a life after it leaves? I walked through the rooms and saw the artifacts: a clock that had stopped, a stack of newspapers from a decade ago, a pair of glasses resting on a windowsill. In the kitchen, there was a table with a worn surface, scarred by years of knives and coffee cups and elbows. I put my hand on it, and I felt something—not literally, but I felt it nonetheless: the weight of all those meals, all those conversations, all those mornings when the light came through the window and fell across the same scarred wood. The table was not valuable. But it was full. It was full of time.

There is a word for this kind of fullness. The Greeks called it kairos—the unstretched moment, the time that is experienced rather than measured. We live mostly in chronos, the time of clocks and calendars, the time that ticks relentlessly forward. But kairos is the time of the dandelion in the crack. It is the time of the old kitchen table. It is the time you enter when you forget to check your phone, when you lose yourself in a conversation or a walk or a task that asks for every part of you. Kairos is not a luxury. It is a necessity. Without it, life becomes a series of tasks, a checklist, a countdown. With it, life becomes something else: a story, a song, a prayer.

I do not want to be romantic about this. Wandering is not always pleasant. Sometimes it leads you into dark places—into grief, into regret, into the small hard rooms of your own disappointments. I have sat by the window on many nights, watching the rain, and felt the full weight of all the things I have failed to do and all the people I have failed to be. But even that, I think, is part of the art. To be fully human is to be able to hold the darkness and the light in the same hand. To wander is to accept that you will not always have a map, and that sometimes the best you can do is to keep moving, step by step, paying attention as you go.

There is a story I like about the Japanese poet Matsuo Bashō. He was traveling through the northern provinces of Japan, on foot, writing haiku as he went. He did not have a destination in the modern sense. He had a direction, and a longing, and an enormous capacity for wonder. When he saw a horse grazing in a field, he wrote a poem. When he saw a snake crossing a road, he wrote a poem. When he saw a temple gate overgrown with moss, he wrote a poem. He was not trying to capture anything. He was letting the world in, and the world filled him until he had to let it out again in words. That is what I want my life to be. Not a series of achievements, but a series of encounters. Not a résumé, but a notebook. Not a destination, but a path—wandering, winding, always showing me something new.

I have started taking walks again. Not the brisk, purposeful walks of exercise, but the slow, aimless walks of a child. I go out without a plan. I turn left or right depending on which tree looks interesting. I stop to watch a crow wrestle with a piece of bread. I sit on a bench and watch the clouds rearrange themselves. I have learned the names of a few wildflowers: queen anne’s lace, chicory, goldenrod. I have learned to identify the call of a blue jay and the rustle of a squirrel in the leaves. These are small things, I know. But they are not nothing. They are the opposite of nothing. They are the threads out of which a life is woven, and I had forgotten how much thread I was letting slip through my fingers.

The strange thing is that this wandering has made me more productive, not less. By giving myself permission to be idle, I have given my mind permission to work on its own schedules. Ideas arrive when I am not looking for them. Solutions come when I am not forcing them. It is as if the mind is a river, and I had been trying to dam it with effort; when I stopped, when I let it flow, it found its own way to the sea. I wonder how many breakthroughs, personal and collective, are lost to us because we are too busy to wander. I wonder how many inventions, how many poems, how many acts of kindness are waiting in the margins of our attention, in the moments we dismiss as wasted.

There is a phrase in the Christian tradition: “pray without ceasing.” I have never been able to take that literally, but I think I understand it now. To pray without ceasing is to live in a state of constant openness to the world. It is to see the divine in the ordinary, the sacred in the mundane. It is to treat every encounter, every object, every breath as an occasion for gratitude. And gratitude, I think, is the root of everything. When I crouched on the sidewalk and looked at that dandelion, I felt a flood of gratitude—not for the dandelion itself, exactly, but for the fact that I had been given the chance to see it. For the fact that the world is so endlessly, abundantly full of things worth noticing. For the fact that I am alive, in this moment, in this body, on this earth, with all its cracks and all its flowers.

We live in a time that tells us to hurry. To do more, to be more, to consume more. But I have come to believe that the most radical act we can perform is to slow down. To stop. To look. To wander. To let the moment unfold without forcing it to be something else. The dandelion did not ask for my attention. It simply grew, in the crack, in the concrete, in the light of the dying day. And when I gave it my attention, it gave me something in return. It gave me a reminder: that life is not in the distance, over the hill, in the future we are always rushing toward. It is here. It is now. It is in the crack. It is in the flower. It is in the hand that reaches down to touch a leaf, and the breath that carries the faint scent of rain, and the heart that, for one brief moment, is entirely present.

So this is my small gospel, if you can call it that: wander more. Not physically, necessarily. Mentally. Emotionally. Spiritually. Let your thoughts go where they want, even if they are afraid. Look at the things you have always taken for granted as if you are seeing them for the first time. Sit with the uncomfortable silences. Wait for the world to speak to you, and when it does, listen. You will not get a second chance at this moment. This moment, right now, is already slipping away. The only way to hold it is to notice it. The only way to keep it is to let it go, and in the letting go, to be fully there.

I have not reached the end of my wandering. I do not expect to. The path unfolds as I walk, and it will continue to unfold long after I am gone. But I am learning, slowly, to trust it. To trust the cracks in the sidewalk. To trust the wildflowers and the weeds. To trust the old kitchen tables and the empty houses and the rain on the window. To trust that if I pay attention, the world will show me what I need to see. And perhaps, in some small way, that is enough. Perhaps that is everything. The art of wandering is the art of being alive. And it is never too late to begin.

## In Praise of the Unnoticed

The path through the park was the same path I had taken a hundred times, which is precisely why I did not see it. My feet knew the way, my eyes were elsewhere—on the small illuminated rectangle in my palm, where the day’s grievances and amusements flowed past like a river of glass beads. I was engaged in that most modern of occupations: absorbing information while experiencing nothing. The sun was setting, or rising, I could not have said which; the light was merely a condition, not a presence. And then, because the sidewalk buckled at one familiar spot, I stumbled, and in the moment of looking down to recover my balance, I saw it: a single dandelion, not in a bed or a border, but thrusting through a crack in the concrete, its head a perfect geometry of yellow florets. I stopped. I put the phone away. I knelt, with the unselfconsciousness of a child—or a fool—and looked.

That dandelion did something to me. It was not a revelation; it was not beautiful in any transcendent sense. It was simply there, entire, alive, indifferent to my dramas. And I realized, with a small shock, that I had not truly looked at a plant in weeks. I had seen lawns, trees, flowerbeds—they registered as background furniture. But I had not *encountered* a living thing. I had not allowed a leaf to fill my whole field of vision, to trace its veins, to wonder at the cellular ferocity that pushed it through asphalt. In that moment the dandelion was not a weed; it was a lesson. It said, as plainly as anything can say: you are missing the world.

This is not an original confession. It is the confession of an age. We live, as every commentator reminds us, in an economy of attention, where our minds are the raw material extracted by algorithms and monetized by advertisers. The metaphors we use are industrial: we talk of *scrolling*, *streaming*, *surfing*—all movement, all flow, all restless locomotion across surfaces. What we rarely talk about is stillness. What we rarely talk about is the act of stopping. Attention has become a scarce resource, not because we are incapable of concentrating, but because we have trained ourselves out of the habit. We have outsourced our curiosity to recommendation engines. We have let the world be mediated, curated, and delivered to us in packets, each one designed to be slightly more gripping than the last. And the price of this convenience is the erasure of the incidental, the overlooked, the slow—all the small wonders that make a life feel inhabited rather than merely operated.

I used to know this. As a child, I did not need to be taught to pay attention; I had not yet learned to be distracted. I remember a creek behind my grandmother’s house, a narrow ribbon of brown water that any adult would have dismissed as drainage. But to me it was an ocean. I would lie on my stomach on the bank for what felt like hours, watching water striders skate across the surface tension, their feet dimpling the film without breaking it. I would scoop up handfuls of mud and sift for worms, for the translucent eggs of snails, for the tiny armored triops that would appear, like visitors from another epoch, in the warm shallows. The world was not backdrop; it was a dense, buzzing, infinite text, and I was learning to read it with my whole body. I felt time not as a line but as a pool, deep and still. An afternoon could contain a thousand years.

What happened to that child? The usual things. School happened, with its bells and schedules, its insistence on one subject at a time and its implicit lesson that knowledge is something you acquire at a desk, not something you encounter in a creek. Puberty happened, bringing the terrible self-consciousness that turns every glance outward into a mirror. Technology happened, first television, then the internet, then the smartphone, each one more adept than the last at filling the empty spaces where noticing used to grow. And slowly, incrementally, I replaced the world with representations of the world. I did not stop seeing; I stopped *looking*. The difference is not semantic. To see is to register light on the retina. To look is to bring the full weight of one’s attention to bear on something, to ask it questions, to wait for answers. Looking is a kind of conversation. Seeing is just a transaction.

The dandelion stopped me, but it did not save me. That would be too neat. What it did was remind me that I had a choice. Attention, I have come to believe, is not a fixed capacity but a muscle, and like any muscle it can be strengthened, or it can atrophy. The act of noticing is a discipline, one of the oldest in the world, though we tend to hide it under other names. The artist’s discipline, the scientist’s discipline, the mystic’s discipline—all are, at bottom, the same practice: sustained, open, patient attention to what is present. The haiku poet who writes about a frog jumping into an old pond is not being whimsical; she is doing the most serious work there is, the work of registering the exact texture of an instant. The naturalist who sits motionless for an hour to watch a bird build its nest is not wasting time; he is participating in the vast, slow conversation of life. The contemplative who repeats a single word for decades is not trying to empty the mind, but to fill it—with the ordinary, the immediate, the sacred-in-the-common.

The great teachers of attention are often the most surprising. Consider the Japanese artist and essayist Tanizaki, who wrote a whole book in praise of shadows, arguing that beauty is not something you add to a room but something you reveal by allowing darkness to remain. He was not talking about interior design; he was talking about a mode of perception. To notice shadows is to notice the spaces between things, the quiet places that modern life is always trying to eliminate with more light, more noise, more signal. Or consider the naturalist Bernd Heinrich, who spent years studying ravens and discovered that they imitate predators and play with objects—not because they are foraging, but because they are curious. Curiosity, in Heinrich’s ravens, is not a means to an end; it is an end in itself. That is what attention looks like when it is not enslaved to utility. It is a form of play.

I began, after the dandelion, to experiment. I would take walks without my phone, and instead of listening to a podcast or a playlist, I would listen to the place itself—the wind in the sycamores, the scolding of a jay, the distant hum of a lawnmower, the way my own breathing changed as I climbed a hill. At first this was excruciating. The absence of stimulation felt like withdrawal, and in a sense it was. My brain, conditioned to novelty, kept reaching for a pocket that was vacant. But after a week or two, something shifted. The sounds began to separate, to acquire texture and location. I could hear the difference between a finch and a sparrow, not because I had learned their calls from an app, but because I had sat still long enough to notice that one song rises while the other falls. I began to see the same differentiation in the visual field. The park, which had been a green blur, resolved into distinct biographies: the oak with a scar where lightning had split its trunk, the patch of plantain that grew where field mice had disturbed the soil, the dead branch where a pileated woodpecker had hammered into a carpenter-ant nest, leaving chips of wood like blond sawdust on the ground. None of this was useful. All of it was necessary.

The writer and farmer Wendell Berry has a phrase: “the peace of wild things.” He wrote a short poem of that title, in which he lies down in the grass and lets the wild things—the wood drake, the great heron—restore his soul. But what strikes me about that poem is that Berry does not merely lie down. He *watches*. The wood drake is not an emblem; it is a bird. The heron is not a symbol; it is a bird, feeding in the shallows. The poem works because Berry’s attention is specific. He does not say “I saw some birds and felt calm.” He says, “I come into the peace of wild things who do not tax their lives with forethought of grief.” The wild things are at peace precisely because they are not elsewhere. They are entirely where they are. To watch them is to be invited, for a moment, into that same state.

This is the discipline of noticing, and it has a moral dimension that we often overlook. Attention is the beginning of care. You cannot love what you do not see. You cannot protect what you have not noticed is endangered. The environmental movement, at its best, has understood this. The reason we protect a wetland is not because of an abstract argument about ecosystem services; it is because someone took the time to wade into it, to see the heron, to hear the chorus of frogs, to be changed by the encounter. The great nature writers—Aldo Leopold, Rachel Carson, Terry Tempest Williams—all make the same move: they render the particular with such vividness that the reader feels complicit in its fate. Leopold’s “thinking like a mountain” begins with a mountain on which he has shot a wolf, and the dying fire in the wolf’s eyes. The essay is a confession of inattention, a testimony to the moment he saw the consequences of not noticing.

And yet, if I am honest, my own rediscovery of attention has not been consistently noble. It has been a struggle, full of lapses. I still catch myself reaching for my phone at red lights. I still drift through conversations, composing responses while the other person is speaking. I still walk through a beautiful landscape with my mind two hours ahead, rehearsing a meeting or replaying an argument. The muscle atrophies quickly; it takes only a few days of neglect to lose the tone I had gained. But the good news is that it strengthens quickly too. A single morning of sitting in the garden, watching the bees work the lavender, is enough to recalibrate my sense of time. The bees do not know the concept of a deadline. They move from flower to flower with a kind of lavish inefficiency, each visit an end in itself. Watching them, I remember that attention is not a resource to be hoarded but a joy to be indulged.

I have found that the practice of noticing spills over into other areas of life, including the most human one: the act of listening. To truly listen to another person is a form of attention that is vanishingly rare. Most of us do not listen; we wait. We wait for the other to finish so that we can speak, or we wait for the pause into which we can insert our advice or our anecdote. But what would it mean to listen without agenda, without the need to reply? What would it mean to hear the other person’s words as if they were the first words ever spoken, as if the speaker were a stranger from a distant country? This is, strangely enough, a spiritual practice. The theologian Paul Tillich said that the first duty of love is to listen. Not to fix, not to solve, not to teach—just to listen. That kind of listening creates space. It says: you are here. Your experience matters. I am willing to be changed by your account of the world.

I tried this once, deliberately, with an elderly neighbor. She was a woman I had avoided for years because she talked slowly and at length about her garden, her children, her ailments. I had categorized her as boring, which is to say, I had not actually heard a word she had said. One afternoon I decided to practice attention. I sat on her porch and listened for an hour. She told me about the peonies her mother had planted in 1948, how she had dug them up and moved them three times, how they always bloomed on her birthday regardless of the weather. She told me about her husband, dead twenty years, who had been a lineman for the electric company, how he had fallen off a pole in a storm and broken his back, how he had never complained and had built her a greenhouse with his own hands while still in a body cast. She told me about the mockingbird that had learned to imitate the sound of the school bus’s air brakes, and how it had fooled her every morning for a month. When I left, I felt as if I had traveled to another country. None of this information was useful. All of it was vital. She was not boring; I was bored, which is its own kind of blindness.

There is a word in Japanese, *yūgen*, that is often translated as “profound, mysterious beauty,” but which really refers to the sense of deep meaning that lies beneath the surface of ordinary things. To perceive *yūgen* is to feel, in the presence of a sunset or a single autumn leaf on a stone, the vastness of time, the fragility of existence, the interweaving of all life. It is not something you can grasp; it is something that grasps you. But I believe it is more available than we think. It does not require a trip to a remote mountain or a cathedral. It requires only the willingness to stop, to look, to listen. To notice the way light falls on a kitchen table at 4 p.m. To notice the crumbs of yesterday’s bread still in the grain of the wood. To notice the sound of your own breathing, which you have carried with you every moment of your life and almost never heard.

The essayist Rebecca Solnit begins her book *A Field Guide to Getting Lost* with a meditation on the word “lost.” She writes that “lost” once meant not only being unable to find your way but also being “occult, or hidden, or secret.” To be lost is to be caught in a state of not-knowing, which can be terrifying, but which is also the condition of discovery. I wonder if our age is lost in the more obvious sense—overwhelmed, anxious, unable to find a path through the noise. And I wonder if the remedy is not more navigation but more attention. To be present is, paradoxically, to be found. When I am sitting on the damp ground looking at a dandelion, I know exactly where I am: in a body, on a planet, at one moment in a chain of moments that stretches back to the first cell and forward to whatever will come after. That knowledge does not solve anything. It is not a plan or an answer. But it is a ground. It is a place to stand.

The dandelion has gone, of course. It was mowed down the next week by the city crew, who saw it as a weed and not as a messenger. But its offspring are scattered across the park, and each spring brings a new generation. I pass the old crack in the sidewalk on my walks, and sometimes I stop to see what has moved in: a tuft of crabgrass, a prostrate knotweed, a small and nameless moss. The crack is a memorial to my rediscovery of the obvious: that the world is always offering itself to us, in infinite detail, and that we are the ones who turn away. We are the ones who choose the screen over the sky, the algorithm over the avenue, the feed over the field. It does not have to be that way. We can choose to look. We can choose to listen. We can choose, one small act of attention at a time, to return to the living world.

On my darker days, I wonder if this is enough. There is so much suffering, so much injustice, so much deliberate cruelty being done to the earth and to one another. What good is watching a bee? What difference does one person’s noticing make against the roar of the machinery? And then I remember that every movement for justice, every act of compassion, every repair of a broken thing began with someone noticing. Someone looked at a polluted river and said, “This is not right.” Someone looked at an overcrowded classroom, an unsafe workplace, a dying patient, a wounded soldier, and refused to look away. Attention is the first act of love and the first act of politics. To notice is to be implicated. Once you have truly seen a thing, you cannot pretend it does not exist. The moral life begins not with principles but with perception.

So I write this as a kind of letter to myself, a reminder that the world is still here. The sun is still setting, not on a screen but in the sky, where it does every evening with a lightshow that no algorithm can capture. The heron is still standing in the shallows, patient as a lesson. The ants are still moving their eggs along the cracked sidewalk, ceaseless as thought. The voice of my neighbor is still speaking, if I will only sit and listen. None of these things will make the news. None of them will trend. But they are, in a much truer sense, the news: the ongoing, unspeakable, miraculous fact of existence. To attend to them is to practice a form of resistance—not against anything, but for everything. For the leaf. For the bird. For the other person who is, right now, trying to tell you something. For the life that is not somewhere else but here, not someday but now, not in the feed but in the flesh. We can walk out of the house with our eyes open. We can let the dandelion stop us. We can stay, for as long as it takes, to be present to what is present. That is all. That is everything.

samples.result:
**Maps of the Unseen: A Meditation on Walking, Memory, and the City**

There is a particular kind of silence that descends on a city late on a Sunday afternoon, when the shops have closed and the offices are empty, and the only other souls on the street are the ones who have nowhere to be. It is in this liminal hour that I most often find myself walking, not with any destination in mind, but with the loose, unbuckled gait of a thought trying to find its way out of a labyrinth. Walking, for me, has never been merely a way of getting from one point to another. It is a way of reading the world, a way of listening to the hum beneath the surface, a way of committing to memory the things that maps leave out.

I think of the city as a vast palimpsest, a manuscript that has been written over so many times that the old letters bleed through the new. Every street corner holds the ghost of an earlier version of itself, and every walk is a stroll through the margins of these edits. On my own street, a half-mile stretch that runs from a shuttered bakery to a car repair shop, I can trace the history of the neighborhood in the façades. The bakery’s sign is still there, painted in faded blue, but the windows are papered over with a notice of a liquor license application. The repair shop has been there for forty years, its owner a man named Felix who knows more about the city’s underground drainage system than any civil engineer. Above the shop, the brickwork reveals two rows of windows that were bricked up sometime in the 1920s, when the building was converted from a mill to warehousing. If I stand still long enough, I can almost hear the looms, and the smell of oil that used to hang over the district, a smell that has been replaced by the tang of fast food and bus exhaust.

This is the city as palimpsest, and walking is the only way to read it. You cannot see these layers from a car; the speed of traffic flattens the world into a series of blurry signposts. You cannot see them from a bus, either, unless you happen to be looking out the window at exactly the right moment. But on foot, you have the luxury of time, the luxury of stopping to look at a gatepost that carries the initials of a Victorian merchant, or to read a brass plaque that commemorates a scandalous trial that took place in a building that is now a pretzel shop. The flâneur, that figure of the nineteenth-century Parisian boulevardier described by Baudelaire, was the first to articulate this mode of city-knowing. He was a wanderer who observed the spectacle of urban life, but who also remained an anonymous part of it. He was, in Walter Benjamin’s terms, a "botanist of the asphalt," a collector of impressions who delighted in the random and the incidental. To walk as a flâneur is to decline the imperative of efficiency. It is to treat the city not as a network of journeys to be completed, but as a field of possibility.

I prefer to walk without a map, or rather, with a mental map that has been scribbled over so many times that it resembles the notebooks of a mad cartographer. There is a joy in getting lost, in following a street that looks intriguing and discovering a cul-de-sac that ends in a patch of wildflowers, or a narrow alley that opens onto a courtyard with a single, ancient chestnut tree. Once, I turned a corner that I had never turned before and found a small, unswept square, nestled between the rear walls of a shopping center and the side of a church. In the center of the square was a stone obelisk, covered in lichen, with a date (1821) and an inscription in French that had been almost worn away. I later learned that this was a milestone on the old Paris road, a remnant of the royal postal route. For years, I had been traveling along the modern highway parallel to it, never knowing that I was passing within fifty yards of a fragment of the eighteenth century. The lesson was simple: the city is never wholly known. There is always a hidden layer, an unvisited corner, a forgotten stairway.

But walking is not just about the external world; it sets the internal one in motion. There is a deep, bodily connection between the rhythm of the feet and the drift of the mind. Nietzsche, who knew a thing or two about both, wrote: "All truly great thoughts are conceived while walking." He was not exaggerating. The steady, repetitive motion of walking frees the brain from the tyranny of focused attention, allowing thoughts to surface that would otherwise remain buried under the noise of the day. It is no accident that many philosophers and writers have been devoted walkers. Rousseau took walks to improvise his texts; Dickens would famously walk the streets of London at night, obsessively, sometimes twenty miles at a stretch; and Virginia Woolf used her morning walks through Bloomsbury to sort out the tangled threads of her novels. The body moves, the heart beats a little faster, the blood carries oxygen to the brain, and suddenly the solution to a problem that has been nagging at you all day appears, unbidden, like a bird landing on a branch. I have solved more practical dilemmas on a two-hour walk through an ordinary subdivision than I ever have at a desk. The desk is a place of worry, of staring at the blank screen. The sidewalk is a place of flow, of ideas rising and falling like the breath.

The science, for what it is worth, backs this up. Studies have shown that walking, particularly in green spaces, can improve mood, reduce rumination, and enhance creative problem-solving. But the science is secondary. The real point is phenomenological: when you walk, you are fully present in your body, and the mind follows suit. There is a reason we say "let me think it over on foot." The phrase is not just a colloquialism. It is a recognition that the process of thinking, of deliberating, of weighing one thing against another, is somehow tied to the beat of the feet on the pavement. The body and the mind are not separate, and the act of walking stitches them together into a single, fluid gesture.

Yet the walker’s attention is a fragile thing. In the age of the smartphone, we walk with our heads down, our eyes fixed on a screen, our earbuds streaming a podcast or a playlist. We pass by the faded sign, the bricked-up windows, the obscure obelisk, and we see none of it. The city becomes a backdrop, a series of obstacles to be navigated while we continue our digital conversation. The art of noticing, which is the soul of walking, is lost. I am as guilty of this as anyone. There are days when I have walked to the pharmacy and back with my phone in my hand, my mind somewhere else entirely, and I realize that I have no memory of the walk at all. The streets were there, but I was not. The philosopher of attention, William James, once wrote that the faculty of voluntarily bringing back a wandering attention, over and over again, is the very root of judgment, character, and will. Walking without a phone is an exercise in this kind of deliberate attention. It is a way of training the mind to be present, to notice the small, odd, beautiful, and melancholy things that line every street if we have the eyes to see them.

What are those small things? On a typical walk, if I am not careful, I miss them. But when I am careful, the world opens up like a pop-up book. There is a patch of pavement near the church where the asphalt has bubbled and cracked, and in the cracks, there are dandelions and shepherd’s purse growing, tiny green shoots pushing through the grit. The city is full of this persistence of nature, of life asserting itself in the most improbable places. There is a drainpipe that has been bent by a delivery truck, and now, when it rains, it spouts a fountain that arcs over the sidewalk. There is a window on the third floor of an office building that always has a cat sitting in it, a tabby who regards me with the indifference of a citizen of a more sufficient world. There is the sound of a saxophone coming from an open window near the old mill, always the same melancholy phrase, played over and over, as if the musician is practicing a phrase that has become his own. These are the facts that never make it into the guidebooks. They are the coordinates of a personal map, a map of the unseen.

Walking in a new city is a radically different experience. You have no mental map, no shortcuts, no habitual routes. Every intersection is a decision, every street a question. Your body is alert in a way it is not when you are at home; you notice the names on the street signs, the shape of the lampposts, the accent of the people who pass by. I remember a walk in Lisbon one rainy evening, when I left my hotel with no plan and ended up in the maze of alleyways below the castle. I was hopelessly lost, but it did not matter. The rain had driven away all but the most determined pedestrians, and I found myself on a terrace overlooking the Tagus river, the lights of the city flickering below me like a map of stars. That moment was not on any itinerary. It was a gift of the lost walk, a reward for surrendering to the city's own logic. In a familiar city, the danger is that we stop seeing. We walk the same route with our eyes half-closed, our mind on our to-do list. The challenge of the flâneur is to bring the tourist's fresh eyes to the everyday. To see your own block as if you had just arrived; to walk your own street as if you had never seen it before. This is not easy. It requires a deliberate effort of defamiliarization, a willingness to look at the ordinary as if it were strange. But the reward is a renewed sense of wonder.

The city also changes its character with the hours. To walk at dawn is to see the city as a stage before the actors arrive. The streets are clean, or at least cleaner than they will be. The light is pale, the air is soft, and the only sounds are the clatter of a milk truck and the distant hiss of the central heating plant. The sunrise is a secret shared by the few who are up: the newspaper delivery woman, the jogger with the golden retriever, the man who is sweeping the steps of the bank even though it will not open for three hours. There is an intimacy to these encounters. You nod to each other, a silent recognition of the temporary tribe of the early rising. To walk at night, on the other hand, is to see the city through a different lens. The crowds are gone, the traffic is thin, and the architecture is transformed by the sodium-orange lamplight into a set of theatrical silhouettes. You see the shadows more than the buildings. The streetlights create pools of light among the dark, and in those pools, you are briefly visible, a solitary figure. The city at night is uncanny. It is both familiar and strange. The door of the laundromat that was open during the day is now barred. The café where you read a book yesterday is now a darkened cage of tables and chairs. The city is not sleeping; it is dreaming, and you are a dream-walker in it.

The social dimension of walking is equally rich. On foot, we belong to the city in a way we do not when we are encased in a car. We brush past strangers, accidentally make eye contact, exchange a brief "sorry" or "excuse me." There are the beggars and street musicians, who are part of the city’s texture as much as any building. There are the regulars: the man who walks his poodle every evening at six, the woman who sits on the same bench every morning with a book that she never seems to read, the group of teenagers who cluster around the bus stop with the energy of wild animals. These are the characters of the neighborhood, and though we never speak, we are engaged in a kind of silent drama, a shared performance of urban life. I have come to know my city’s moods better than I know my own hometown, because the hometown was a place I was driven through, while the city is a place I have walked through. The car isolates us; the sidewalk connects us. The car turns the landscape into a moving picture; the sidewalk turns it into a stage on which we are both actor and audience.

But these days, the practice of walking is under threat. The design of modern cities has privileged the automobile to the neglect of the pedestrian. We have created suburban landscapes where walking is not just inconvenient but impossible, where the roads have no sidewalks or where they dead-end into a six-lane highway. The shift began in the early twentieth century, with the rise of the car and the expansion of suburbs, and it has continued with the spread of big-box stores and gated communities. The result is that many people grow up without ever having walked to school, or to the store, or to a friend’s house. They have experienced the world through a windshield. They have been denizens of the inside, not the outside. The loss is not simply physical; it is spiritual. When we stop walking, we stop paying attention. When we stop paying attention, we lose our connection to the world, to the texture of our neighborhoods, to the faces of our neighbors. We become strangers in our own communities.

The pandemic, paradoxically, brought some of this back. For a few months in 2020, the streets emptied of cars and filled with people walking. I remember the strange silence of those days, the absence of the constant drone of traffic, the sight of families walking in the middle of the road because there was no traffic to fear. It was a glimpse of a different kind of city, a city where the public realm was truly public, where the street was a place for people, not just for machines. Many of us took walks then as a way of escaping the claustrophobia of our homes, and we discovered that walking was not just a form of exercise but a form of companionship, a way of being outside while still being alone. The memory of that brief, strange spring has stayed with me. It made me realize how much we had lost, but also how quickly we could take it back if we chose to.

The slow movement, which began as a protest against the homogenization of food culture, has a parallel in the world of urban space. To walk slowly, without a destination, without a purpose, is a kind of rebellion against the speed culture that defines modernity. It is a refusal to treat time as a commodity to be optimized. It is a statement that there is value in the journey, in the act of moving through the world with no imperative other than to look and to be. The Situationists, a group of French artists and thinkers in the 1950s and 60s, developed the practice of the dérive, or the drift, which involved walking through a city for no other reason than to let the landscape of the city guide you, to be led by the magnetic pulls of urban architecture, the contrasts, the hidden passages, the decaying neighborhoods. They believed that by drifting, one could break through the "spectacle" of consumer culture and uncover the authentic emotional geography of the city. Their ideas were playful, but they had a serious core. They understood that the way we move through space shapes the way we think and feel. They understood that walking is a way of reclaiming the city from the planners and the developers, of making it our own.

I think of my own walks as a kind of derive. Sometimes I choose a direction based on a whim: tonight, I will follow the scent of jasmine. Sometimes I choose to cross the river at a new bridge, to see what the city looks like from a different angle. Sometimes I just let the wind decide, letting my body be pushed along by the same force that moves the leaves and the sea. This is a kind of play, and play is important. It is a way of staying alive to the world, of keeping oneself from the hardening of the arteries that comes with routine. The walker is always a child, seeing the city for the first time, even if they have walked the same route a thousand times. The secret is to see, not to look. To notice the slight variations: the new graffiti on the wall, the fallen branch that was not there yesterday, the shop window that has been redone, the woman who is walking a different dog today than last week. The city is alive; it is changing every day. The walker is a witness to these changes, a reporter of the small news that never makes the headlines.

And what is the point of all this walking, all this noticing? Is it simply a form of recreation, a pleasant way to spend an hour? I think it is more than that. It is a way of embodying the idea that we are not just cogs in a machine, but finite beings with a relationship to the places we inhabit. To walk is to take up space, to leave an imprint, to be physically present. It is to say, "I am here, and I care about this corner of the world." The city, after all, is made of love as much as of concrete. It is measured not in miles but in memories, in the benches where we sat, the doorways where we sheltered from the rain, the sidewalks that we wore down with our feet. The walker is the keeper of these memories. They are the guardian of the city’s soul, the one who refuses to let it become a mere collection of buildings and signs.

So I will continue to walk. I will walk on the Sunday afternoons of the quiet, and on the rainy Tuesday mornings, and on the sweltering afternoons when the heat shimmers off the asphalt. I will walk with or without a destination. I will walk in my own neighborhood and in cities far away. And each time, I will discover that the city is not a map of streets but a map of the unseen, a map of the stories that are never told, the details that are never photographed, the moments that hover on the edge of memory. To walk is to live in the richness of the present, to feel the pulse of the city beneath your feet. I invite you to join me. Put on your shoes. Leave your phone at home. Step outside. The world is waiting, one step at a time.

**In Praise of Drifting**

The rain began at three in the afternoon, not with the theatrical crackle of a summer storm but as a slow, patient argument that the sky was having with the pavement. I was sitting in a café that had once been a butcher’s shop, eavesdropping on the leaky gutters and pretending to read a book I had already read twice. The book lay open on the table, its spine cracked, its margins filled with the hieroglyphs of earlier selves. I had come to that café because the wifi was weak, because the coffee was strong, and because I had decided, in a rare fit of self-respect, to spend an hour doing nothing that could be measured. The decision felt unlawful, like crossing a border without papers.

We live in a civilization that worships the arrow: goals, metrics, optimization, the relentless trajectory from point A to point B. Every hour is a budget line; every thought is a potential investment. There is an app for tracking sleep, an app for tracking water, an app for tracking the number of times we check our phones, which exists to shame us into checking our phones less, which we use while checking our phones. Efficiency has become the secular religion of the modern world, and its parishioners are never at rest. Idleness is a sin, boredom a failure of spirit, and the word “wandering” has been reduced to a metaphor for losing a tennis match.

But I have always been fond of the wrong turns. I suspect the map of a life is not a straight line but a tangle of loops, curls, and cul-de-sacs — a doodle that only makes sense when you lift the pen and step back. The people I admire most are not the ones who marched unerringly toward a single summit, but those who kept veering off the path to sniff the air, to paddle in the shallows, to ask a stranger about the weather. They understood that the destination is a rumor, and the journey is the only thing you can actually feel with your feet.

I was thinking of my own childhood walks home from school. The route was a simple triangle — three streets, two corners, one crossing guard who wore his fluorescent vest like a royal mantle. But I transformed it into an epic cartography. There was the alley behind the garages where moss grew like a green language on the bricks. There was the storm drain that sang after rain, a tinny, gurgling hymn. There was the fence with the loose board, behind which a plump cat named something unknowable lived its secret life. I would walk slowly, deliberately, trailing my fingers against walls, kicking stones that became planets. The stones were not “wasted time.” They were the raw material of an inner world. The twenty minutes of the walk were a cathedral of daydream, and I entered it every afternoon without a passport.

Somewhere along the way, I lost that cathedral. It wasn’t a single catastrophic loss, like a fire or a bankruptcy. It was more a gradual erosion, a hundred tiny surrenders to the logic of the arrow. The walks became commute. The commute became scrolling. The scrolling became a kind of restless meditation on all the things I wasn’t doing. The mind, once a meadow of loose associations, became a checklist. I began to measure my days in the currency of completion: emails sent, tasks crossed off, miles logged, hours of “deep work” banked. Even my leisure was managed, optimized, turned into a series of productivity playlists. I had become fluent in the language of the arrow, and I was proud of it.

And yet. And yet.

There is a reason that the greatest thinkers have often been the greatest wasters of time. Archimedes discovered the principle of buoyancy not in a laboratory but in a bath, where he had gone, presumably, to wash and not to solve a physics problem. Newton developed his theories of motion during a plague-enforced exile from Cambridge, when he was left alone with nothing but an orchard and his own wandering thoughts. Darwin took long daily walks around a path called the Sandwalk, and though he claimed the exercise was merely a pastime, he was known to pause for minutes at a time, staring at a beetle or into the abyss, letting the machinery of the mind grind in some secret, subterranean way. The stories may be apocryphal in detail, but they point to a deep truth: insight often arises not from concentrated effort but from its opposite. When we stop yanking at the thread, the knot sometimes loosens itself.

Modern cognitive science has a name for what happens during these idle moments. It calls it the default mode network, a vast constellation of brain regions that hums into activity when we are not focused on a task — when we are daydreaming, woolgathering, letting our minds slip the leash of intention. In this state, the brain does not rest. It churns. It connects distant memories, rehearses future scenarios, generates novel combinations, tells itself stories. It is, in many ways, the engine of creativity. But the default mode network is also fragile. It cannot compete with the dopamine-driven clamor of a smartphone. Every buzz, every ping, every compulsive swipe yanks the mind back into the spotlight of attention, where it must process incoming stimuli in real time, leaving no room for the slow, asynchronous alchemy of drift. We have filled the cathedral with slot machines, and we wonder why we no longer feel awe.

I am as guilty as anyone. I have stood in breathtaking landscapes and felt the urge to photograph them, not because I wanted to remember, but because I wanted to prove I was there — as if the experience itself were insufficient without a receipt. I have watched sunsets through a screen, their colors flattened into a rectangle of pixels, while my eyes paid homage to a flawed proxy. I have stayed up late reading arguments with strangers in comment sections, scrolling through the same handful of outrage-reactions, convinced that this was engagement with the world when it was only engagement with a mirror. The world is noisy, but the noisiest noise is the one inside my own pocket.

It was Pascal who wrote that all of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone. I used to read that as a counsel against distraction, a stern injunction to cultivate stillness. But I have begun to think that Pascal had it only half right. The problem is not merely an inability to sit quietly; it is an inability to sit quietly *without a purpose*. We have turned stillness itself into a performance, a box to check on the to-do list of wellness. We attend meditation retreats and track our “streaks” on apps, determined to achieve zero thoughts as efficiently as possible. But the mind is not a machine that should be switched off. It is a waterway. It wants to meander.

The meander is the shape of most living things. Rivers do not flow in straight lines; they curve, they braid, they pool, they carve oxbows that eventually cut themselves off and become silent crescents of slow water. Blood vessels branch like trees. Lightning forks. Even the path of a human life, if you trace it honestly, is not a line but a trail of breadcrumbs, some of them dropped on purpose, most of them scattered by chance. The English word “wander” comes from the Old English *wandrian*, which is related to the root meaning to turn, to wind, to change direction. It is kin to “windlass” and “winding.” To wander is to follow the way the world turns, not to impose a course upon it.

I decided, a few years ago, to rebuild my capacity for wandering. It was not easy. The anxiety that attends purposelessness is physical; it feels like a phantom limb of obligation. I would step out my front door with no destination, and immediately my mind would scream: *What are you doing? This is inefficient. Turn back. Check the news. Check your list.* It took weeks of patient practice to silence the accountant in my head. I learned to leave my phone at home, or at least in my pocket with the ringer off. I learned to make a rule: no maps, no clocks, no agenda. The first few walks were agonizing. I walked ten minutes in one direction, twenty in another. I stared at windows, at gardens, at the uncharted geography of neighborhood trees. I began to notice things: a door painted the impossible blue of a June sky; a forgotten tennis shoe dangling from a power line like a relic of a vanished god; an old man on a porch feeding a pigeon with the solemnity of a priest. The world had been there all along, patient as a houseplant, waiting for me to stop scrolling long enough to see it.

What happened next surprised me. The walks became less a exercise in discipline and more a form of nourishment. I would return home with my head full of half-formed sentences, with solutions to problems I had not consciously been pondering, with a strange, buoyant sadness that was not unpleasant. It was as though the mind had been given back its natural appetite. It had been starving, and I had been feeding it potato chips and energy drinks. I had forgotten that it also needed grapes and dark bread and water that tastes of limestone.

J.R.R. Tolkien once wrote that “not all those who wander are lost.” The line has been repeated so often that it has become a greeting-card motto, the sort of sentiment you see tattooed on forearms and printed on inspirational posters. But like most clichés, it has a genuine heart. The opposite of wandering is not arriving; it is being pinned. It is the condition of the pinned insect, the glassed exhibit, the cursor frozen on a desktop. To wander is to acknowledge that you do not know where you are going, and to be at peace with that ignorance. It is the beginning of humility. It is the recognition that the universe is larger than your plans, and that the best days are often the ones in which nothing was achieved and everything was received.

I have a friend who defines a successful walk as one in which she gets lost at least once. She used to live in Paris, and she would spend her Sundays in the outer arrondissements, deliberately taking the wrong métro line, walking until she no longer recognized the shopfronts, then finding her way back by sun and memory. The stories she tells from those walks are not about landmarks. They are about encounters: a baker who gave her a day-old croissant; a courtyard where an opera singer was practicing scales; a tiny museum dedicated to locks and keys, which she entered and never forgot. She did not accumulate these experiences by checking a list. She accumulated them by letting the city draft her itinerary.

There is a political dimension to this, too. The arrow culture is not merely personal; it is structural. Schools teach to standardized tests. Employers measure productivity in keystrokes and billable hours. Social media platforms monetize our attention. The economy wants us to be predictable, measurable, maximally efficient consumers of work and content. Wandering is a quiet rebellion against all that. It is a refusal to be optimized. It is a statement that the human soul retains the right to its own interiority, its own rhythms, its own time.

In recent years, I have come to see my walks not as a retreat from the world but as a more genuine form of engagement with it. When I used to rush, I experienced only a blur — a compressed montage of crosswalks and buildings, a surface without texture. When I wander, I encounter the world in its particularity. I notice that the barber on the corner has put up a string of Christmas lights in August. I notice that the lilac bushes outside the library are bursting with bees. I notice the sound of a distant train and the way it enters my daydream and becomes a scene involving a stranger who is running away from her own wedding, or a smuggler carrying a suitcase full of books. These stories are worthless in economic terms. No one will pay me for them. And yet they are the very texture of being alive.

The rain had stopped, though I did not notice at first. The café had emptied. The barista was wiping the counter with a cloth, moving in slow circular patterns. I closed my book, paid for my coffee, and stepped outside. The air was greener than before, rinsed and translucent. The pavement was covered with a mosaic of wet leaves. I could see a crack in the clouds, a seam of pale gold light, and I decided, quite deliberately, to follow it. I did not know where it would lead. The street curved left, then right, then opened into a small square I had never noticed in years of passing through the neighborhood. There was a fountain in the center, dry but beautiful, bordered by chipped stone benches. I sat down. I watched a pigeon take a bath in the bowl of water left by the rain. I thought about the book I had not read, the work I had not done, and the extraordinary luxury of being able to sit there, doing nothing, with no claim on my attention except the slow, swelling music of the ordinary.

There is an old word for this state, one that has been pushed to the margins of our vocabulary: “to while.” As in “to while away the hours.” It derives from the Old English *hwīl*, meaning a space of time, a pause, a respite. To while away time is not to kill it but to spend it generously, the way you might spend an afternoon with a beloved friend. It is time in which nothing is produced except the deepening of one’s acquaintance with the world. It is time that leaves no trace except the memory of having moved through the day with attention rather than acceleration.

I stayed on that bench until the light began to change from white to amber. Then I walked home by the long way, passing the barber’s shop, the library, the alley behind the garage. I did not take a single photograph. I did not check my phone. I counted nothing. I had a stupid, wonderful grin on my face, the kind that makes passersby look away. At some point, I crossed a street and was surprised by the color of the brick building in front of me — a warm terracotta that I had seen a hundred times but had never really seen. I know that sounds small. It was small. But smallness is the beginning of scale. From that one brick, I could have walked to the edge of the sea.

We are constantly being told that time is money. I have decided, after many years of believing it, to dissent. Time is not money. Money can be saved, spent, counted, hoarded, lost, and earned. But time does not move in the linear, ledger-like way of currency. It pools and eddies. It loops back on itself. It gives unexpected change. The only way to live with time is to stop trying to optimize it and start trying to inhabit it. And the way to inhabit it is to be present to it — to walk without a destination, to sit without a screen, to let the mind drift into the wild country where thoughts are not tasks and memories are not data.

The sun had set by the time I reached my front door. I stood on the porch for a moment, keys in hand, listening to the evening birds. Somewhere, far off, a dog barked. A car turned down a street and the sound of its engine faded like a held note. I had accomplished nothing that afternoon. I had not transformed the world. I had not been productive. And yet I felt a deep current of contentment, the kind that cannot be manufactured by achievement, only received as a gift. I unlocked the door, went inside, and wrote this down — not because I had to, but because the words were already there, blooming without permission, the way they always do when we finally give them room.

The arc of the world is toward order, or so we tell ourselves: from chaos to form, from scattered to systematized, from wanderer to citizen. But I wonder if the real arc is in the opposite direction. I wonder if we are born knowing how to wander — how to follow a bug with our eyes, how to drift off in the middle of a story, how to spend an hour turning a leaf over and over just because it is shaped like a boat — and then unlearn it, year by year, until we reach adulthood and believe that wandering is a four-letter word. I want to be a heretic. I want to reclaim the meander. I want to sit quietly in a room alone, and to wander loudly through the world, and to remember that every river writes its own name in the land as it goes. There is no destination that is not reached by turning. There is no thought that does not arrive by drifting.

So let the rain fall. Let the light change. Let the path curve away from the map. I intend to follow it — slowly, at last, without an outline — and see where it goes.
